events.title: Convertibility - the peso pegged one-to-one to the dollar
events.detail: The Convertibility Law fixed the peso to the US dollar and required the central bank to back the monetary base with foreign reserves.
events.contested: Ended hyperinflation quickly. It also removed the exchange rate as an adjustment tool, which most accounts treat as central to the 2001 collapse - though the relative weight of the peg, fiscal policy and external shocks is disputed.

events.title: Sovereign default and the end of convertibility
events.detail: Argentina defaulted on roughly US$93bn of sovereign debt, abandoned the peg and froze bank deposits.
events.contested: Restructuring took over a decade and litigation ran to 2016. Argues both ways in the sovereign-debt literature - as evidence that default can be survivable, and as evidence of its lasting cost in market access.
events.refs: ["IMF Independent Evaluation Office, 'The IMF and Argentina, 1991-2001' (2004)"]

events.title: Output collapse: GDP per capita fell 12%
events.detail: Real GDP per capita fell from 10,052 to 8,862 (constant 2015 US$) in a single year.
events.source: derived: World Bank GDP per capita
events.contested: A one-year collapse of this size usually has several causes at once - war, currency crisis, commodity price, or the end of a political order. This marker says it happened; it does not say why.

events.title: Inflation crossed 50% (reached 54%)
events.detail: Consumer price inflation rose from 34.3% to 53.5%, crossing the 50% threshold.
events.source: derived: World Bank consumer price inflation
events.contested: The 50% line is a convention, not a natural boundary. Official inflation statistics are also among the most manipulated numbers governments publish, so the true figure may be higher than the one recorded here.
